statement: As summarized by Sarparast et al. (2022), a few other medicines were each given before MDMA to 14 to 16 healthy adults in single controlled trials. Haloperidol (an antipsychotic, 1.4 mg intravenously; 14 people) did not change the heart-rate, blood-pressure or temperature responses to MDMA but made the state more dysphoric (well-being about 31% lower, state anxiety about 47% higher at 75 minutes, oceanic boundlessness about 59% lower). Methylphenidate (a stimulant; 16 people) delayed MDMA's time to peak by 45.8% without changing its peak (-3.5%) or exposure (+3.2%), raised heart rate by 15.1%, the rate-pressure product by 16.8%, acute complaints by 86.5% and later complaints by 191.9%, and added no psychoactive effect. Carvedilol (a heart and blood-pressure medicine) cut the rise in heart rate by 79.0%, in systolic pressure by 76.9% and in temperature by 42.0% with little change in ratings (any drug effect +7.4%, liking +1.5%) while epinephrine and norepinephrine rose; pindolol, another heart medicine, lowered the peak heart rate by about 17.6% and the overall altered-state score by about 27%; clonidine and doxazosin lowered blood pressure (doxazosin: mean arterial pressure 6.8% lower, with heart rate 9.6% higher); memantine did not change MDMA's memory impairment or mood. The review's table of controlled trials has no entry for MAOIs, mood stabilizers (which include lithium) or anxiolytics with MDMA, and its text says it found no study of benzodiazepines with MDMA. People can feel little from an amount for several reasons (a slow start, as with the delayed peak under methylphenidate; tolerance; a weaker or different product; bodies that differ; a medicine that blunts the effect) and some take more; none of the trials gave more MDMA once the effects were blunted or delayed, so what happens then was not measured. The percentages are the review's, partly read off graphs; the trials were not read for this library; modern MDMA-therapy trials excluded people taking psychiatric medicines or stopped them first; and none of the trials followed people on long-term treatment.
plain: The controlled studies on other psychiatric medicines are few, small (14 to 16 healthy people each) and second-hand, from a 2022 review. Haloperidol, an antipsychotic, left heart rate and blood pressure alone but made people feel worse: less well-being and more anxiety. Methylphenidate, a stimulant, delayed MDMA's peak by about 46 percent, raised heart rate and brought more complaints, with no stronger drug effect. Carvedilol, a heart medicine, cut the rises in heart rate and temperature while ratings stayed about the same. The review lists no controlled study of MAOIs, lithium or benzodiazepines with MDMA. A slow start (methylphenidate delayed the peak) or a medicine that mutes the effect can leave a person feeling little, and some people then take more. None of these trials tested what happens then.
population: Healthy adult volunteers in single laboratory trials of 14 to 16 people each, as summarized by Sarparast et al. (2022)
exposure: A psychiatric or cardiovascular medicine taken before MDMA (study conditions as listed in the review: haloperidol 1.4 mg intravenously; methylphenidate; carvedilol, clonidine, doxazosin, pindolol; memantine 20 mg; MDMA by mouth)
comparator: The same people given a dummy treatment before MDMA
outcome: Rated mood and drug effects, heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, complaints, catecholamines and MDMA blood concentrations
magnitude: As summarized by Sarparast et al. (2022), changes against placebo before MDMA: haloperidol well-being -31% (p<.05), state anxiety +47% at 75 minutes (p<.01), oceanic boundlessness -59% (p<.05), no change in heart rate, blood pressure or temperature; methylphenidate time to peak +45.8% (p<.05), peak -3.5%, exposure +3.2%, heart rate +15.1% and rate-pressure product +16.8% (both p<.001), epinephrine +54.6% (p<.01), acute complaints +86.5% (p<.01), subacute complaints +191.9% (p<.001), any drug effect -1.4%; carvedilol heart-rate rise -79.0%, systolic -76.9% (both p<.001), diastolic -39.2%, temperature -42.0% (p<.05), any drug effect +7.4%, liking +1.5%; pindolol peak heart rate about -17.6% (p<.001), global altered-state score about -26.7% and oceanic boundlessness about -31.9% (both p<.01); clonidine mean arterial pressure -4.5% by the area measure (p<.05); doxazosin mean arterial pressure -6.8% and heart rate +9.6% (p<.05); memantine no effect on memory impairment or mood.

evidence.locator: Table 6, haloperidol rows; Results › MDMA › Antipsychotics and MDMA
evidence.extracted: Haloperidol 1.4 mg intravenously (n=14) did not change cardiovascular or thermogenic responses to MDMA or the startle response, according to the review, but made the state dysphoric: well-being about 31% lower (p<.05), state anxiety about 47% higher at 75 minutes (p<.01), oceanic boundlessness about 59% lower (p<.05). Table 6 lists heart rate 13.7%, systolic pressure 5.0%, diastolic pressure 2.3% and temperature 1.4% higher at 120 minutes, with no significance marks. Values with a tilde were read off graphs by the review's authors.

evidence.locator: Table 6, methylphenidate rows; Results › MDMA › Psychostimulants and MDMA; Discussion › Pharmacodynamic interactions-MDMA, 4th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Methylphenidate (n=16) delayed MDMA's time to peak by 45.8% (p<.05) without changing its peak (-3.5%) or exposure (+3.2%), raised heart rate 15.1% and the rate-pressure product 16.8% (both p<.001) and epinephrine 54.6% (p<.01), and raised acute and subacute complaints by 86.5% (p<.01) and 191.9% (p<.001), without adding psychoactive effects (any drug effect -1.4%).

evidence.locator: Table 6, adrenergic-agent rows (carvedilol, pindolol, clonidine, doxazosin); Results › MDMA › Adrenergic agents and MDMA, 2nd to 5th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Adrenergic agents (n=16 each): carvedilol lowered the heart-rate rise 79.0%, systolic 76.9% (both p<.001), diastolic 39.2% and temperature 42.0% (p<.05), as changes from baseline, with little change in ratings (any drug effect +7.4%, liking +1.5%) while epinephrine (+204.3%) and norepinephrine (+789.7%) rose (both p<.001); pindolol (men) lowered peak heart rate by about 17.6% (p<.001), the global altered-state score by about 26.7% and oceanic boundlessness by about 31.9% (both p<.01) and 'dreaminess' by about 95% (p<.05), with no effect on mean arterial pressure or temperature; clonidine lowered mean arterial pressure by 4.5% by the area measure (p<.05; 27.2% at the peak, not marked significant) and norepinephrine; doxazosin lowered mean arterial pressure 6.8% at the peak (p<.05) but raised heart rate 9.6% (p<.05), and lowered the area of heightened-mood ratings (marked significant). Table 6 gives carvedilol's vital signs as changes from baseline and pindolol's and doxazosin's as raw peaks; values with a tilde were read off graphs. The Discussion calls the effect of clonidine and doxazosin on physiology minimal.

evidence.locator: Table 6, memantine rows; Results › MDMA › Memantine and MDMA
evidence.extracted: Memantine 20 mg (n=15) had no effect on MDMA-induced acute memory impairment or on mood, per the review. Table 6 lists, without significance marks, changes of 0.4 to 13.6% on memory tasks and 0.7 to 41.1% on mood scales, and a 'subjective high' rating 20.9% and 70.3% higher at 90 and 120 minutes; MDMA's level at 1 hour was 1.0% lower.

evidence.locator: Table 4; Discussion › Considerations for future research, 1st and 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Table 4, which lists the controlled trials of psychiatric medicines by class, has no entry in its MDMA column for MAOIs, mood stabilizers (the class that includes lithium) or anxiolytics. The review says it found no study of benzodiazepines with MDMA. Modern MDMA-therapy trials either excluded people taking psychiatric medicines or stopped them first; the review notes that tapering carries its own risks of relapse and discontinuation symptoms. Online communities were described as encouraging olanzapine as a way to end a distressing psychedelic experience; the review says it is unclear whether an atypical antipsychotic would be an appropriate approach.

risk_of_bias.note: The primary trials were not read for this library; the review that reports them appraised none of them and is rated critically low on AMSTAR 2 (study card); some values were read off graphs.

inconsistency.note: Not rated: each medicine rests on one trial.

indirectness.note: Second-hand: numbers come through a review, from healthy volunteers given one dose of the medicine, some by the intravenous route.

imprecision.note: 14 to 16 people per medicine; the review gives no intervals.

grade.reasoning: The primary trials are double-blind, counterbalanced crossovers and start high (METHODS 6.3); the claim reaches them only through a systematic review that did not appraise them, so risk of bias -1 and indirectness -1 are applied, with imprecision -1 for 14 to 16 people each. Certainty very low. Status single-study: each medicine was tested once. Stays at draft because it rests only on the review (METHODS 12, brief). The claim says what was measured and what was not found, never what to do.

verification.flag_note: Rests only on Sarparast et al. (2022) as summarized, until the primary trials are read. The reference records for these trials do not exist. Benzodiazepines, lithium and MAOIs: no controlled study was found by the review; MAOI case reports and deaths are with reader 55; the surveillance odds ratios for olanzapine, risperidone, lithium and benzodiazepines are in the claim on reports.
